(CNN) -- Shark attacks on humans were at the lowest levels in half a decade last year, and a Florida researcher says hard economic times may be to blame. Fewer people in the water means less chance for sharks to attack, ichthyologist George Burgess says. Sharks attacked 59 people in 2008, the lowest number of attacks since 57 in 2003, according to George Burgess, director of the International Shark Attack File, part of the Florida Museum of Natural History on the University of Florida campus in Gainesville. There were 71 attacks in 2007. "One can't help but think that the downturn in the economy played a part in it," Burgess said. Fewer people, especially outside of the United States, have the resources to go to the beach, he said. "To have a shark attack, you have to have humans and sharks in the water at the same time," Burgess said. "If you have a reduction in the number of people in the water, you're going to have a reduction in the opportunities for people and sharks to get together." "We noticed similar declines during the recession that followed the events of 2001, despite the fact that human populations continued to rise," the ichthyologist said. Sharks killed four people in 2008, Burgess said: one in California, one in Australia and two in Mexico. Forty-one of the 59 attacks worldwide came in the United States, and 32 of those occurred in Florida. Surfers accounted for 57 percent of shark attacks, swimmers and waders were the targets in 36 percent of the attacks, and divers the rest, he said. Burgess said the U.S. tends to see more attacks because of a large number of surfers, who are a favorite target of sharks. And neither the economy nor the attacks tend to keep American surfers from practicing their sport. "All they have to do is drive to the beach with the board and get into the water, and the rest is free," he said. And while an attack may make them a bit more wary, he said, "I've yet to find a surfer who says he or she won't go back into the water after a bite or a nip." When the economy improves, shark attack numbers are likely to go up again, according to Burgess, predicting the number of attacks in the next decade will surpass those of the past 10 years. "We're putting so many people in the water that humans are dictating the shark attack situation," he said.

# Shark Attacks Decline as Economic Downturn Keeps Swimmers Ashore

(CNN) -- Shark attacks on humans reached their lowest level in half a decade last year, and one Florida researcher suggests the struggling economy may be a contributing factor. With fewer people entering the water, sharks have had correspondingly fewer opportunities to strike, according to ichthyologist George Burgess.

According to Burgess, director of the International Shark Attack File at the Florida Museum of Natural History on the University of Florida's Gainesville campus, sharks attacked 59 people in 2008—the lowest tally since 57 attacks were recorded in 2003. This marks a notable decline from the 71 attacks reported in 2007.

"One can't help but think that the downturn in the economy played a part in it," Burgess remarked, noting that fewer people—particularly outside the United States—now have the financial means to visit the beach.

"To have a shark attack, you have to have humans and sharks in the water at the same time," he explained. "If you have a reduction in the number of people in the water, you're going to have a reduction in the opportunities for people and sharks to get together." He added that a similar pattern emerged during the recession following the events of 2001, even as global population figures continued to climb.

Sharks were responsible for four fatalities in 2008, according to Burgess: one in California, one in Australia, and two in Mexico. Of the 59 attacks recorded worldwide, 41 occurred in the United States, with 32 of those taking place in Florida alone. Surfers bore the brunt of these encounters, accounting for 57 percent of attacks, while swimmers and waders represented 36 percent, and divers made up the remainder.

Burgess attributed the higher frequency of attacks in the U.S. to its substantial surfing population—a group that sharks seem particularly drawn to. Neither economic hardship nor the risk of attack, he noted, appears to deter American surfers from pursuing their sport. "All they have to do is drive to the beach with the board and get into the water, and the rest is free," he said. While an attack may leave surfers somewhat more cautious, he added, "I've yet to find a surfer who says he or she won't go back into the water after a bite or a nip."

Looking ahead, Burgess anticipates that shark attack numbers will rise again as the economy recovers, predicting that the coming decade will see figures surpass those of the past ten years. "We're putting so many people in the water that humans are dictating the shark attack situation," he concluded.

# Shark Attack Numbers Drop to Five-Year Low, Economy May Be Factor

(CNN) -- Last year saw the fewest shark attacks on record in five years, and according to a researcher based in Florida, the struggling economy could be a contributing cause. Ichthyologist George Burgess explains that with fewer swimmers entering the ocean, sharks simply have less opportunity to strike.

According to Burgess, who heads the International Shark Attack File housed at the Florida Museum of Natural History on the University of Florida's Gainesville campus, sharks bit 59 people throughout 2008 — the smallest tally since 2003's total of 57. This marks a significant drop from 2007, which saw 71 incidents.

"It's hard not to conclude that the economic slowdown contributed to this," Burgess remarked. He noted that many people, particularly those living abroad, simply lack the financial means to visit beaches these days.

Burgess emphasized the basic requirement for any shark encounter: "Both humans and sharks need to occupy the same waters simultaneously for an attack to happen. When fewer swimmers venture into the ocean, naturally there are fewer chances for these two parties to cross paths."

The researcher pointed to a comparable pattern following the 2001 economic downturn, when attack numbers fell even as the global population continued expanding.

Four fatalities resulted from shark encounters in 2008, per Burgess — one victim in California, another in Australia, and two in Mexico. The United States accounted for 41 of the year's 59 total attacks worldwide, with Florida alone responsible for 32 incidents.

Breaking down victim types, surfers made up the majority at 57 percent of all attacks, while swimmers and people wading accounted for 36 percent, leaving divers to comprise the remainder.

Burgess attributes America's higher attack frequency to its substantial surfing population, since surfers represent a particularly appealing target for sharks. Notably, neither financial hardship nor the risk of attack seems to discourage American surfers from pursuing their sport. "The only expenses involved are transportation to the shore and the board itself — everything after that costs nothing," he explained.

Though a shark encounter might make surfers somewhat more cautious, Burgess noted, "I haven't encountered a single surfer yet who says they'll abandon the water permanently after being bitten or nipped."

Looking ahead, Burgess anticipates attack figures will climb once again as economic conditions improve, forecasting that incidents over the coming decade will actually exceed those of the previous ten years. "With so many people entering ocean waters, it's really human behavior that's driving shark attack patterns," he concluded.

According to George Burgess, an ichthyologist and director of the International Shark Attack File, the downturn in attacks can be largely attributed to the global economic recession. Despite the overall global decline, the United States still accounted for the majority of incidents, with 41 of the 59 total attacks occurring within its waters. Interestingly, the data suggests that American surfers did not let the economic downturn keep them out of the water to the same degree as other beachgoers. George Burgess, who oversees the International Shark Attack File at the Florida Museum of Natural History, attributes this decline not to changes in shark behavior or conservation efforts, but to a far more human factor: the global economic downturn.

# The Numbers Behind Shark Attack Statistics: What Experts Say About the Human Factor

When headlines scream about shark attacks, they rarely mention the statistic that matters most: how many people were actually in the water.

According to George Burgess, former director of the Florida Program for Shark Research at the University of Florida and longtime curator of the International Shark Attack File, the surge in reported shark encounters over recent decades has far less to do with sharks becoming more aggressive and far more to do with simple math.

## Correlation, Not Predation

"The point is, whatever is happening in the ocean happens to a bigger population of humans than it did before," Burgess has explained in numerous interviews addressing public shark fears. His research consistently points to a straightforward correlation: as coastal populations grow and beach tourism expands, the raw number of shark encounters rises—not because sharks are hunting more, but because more potential targets are in the water at any given time.

The logic is intuitive once laid out. Sharks patrol coastal waters as part of their natural range, largely indifferent to human presence. When beach attendance was lower—decades ago, before coastal populations boomed and cheap air travel made beach vacations accessible to millions—there were simply fewer chances for a human and a shark to occupy the same few square feet of ocean at the same moment.

## The Denominator Problem

Statisticians call this the "denominator problem." Attack counts alone are nearly meaningless without knowing the size of the population exposed to risk. Burgess and his colleagues at the Shark Attack File have long argued that raw attack numbers should never be reported without context about beach attendance, water sports participation, and coastal population growth.

Florida, for instance, consistently ranks as the location with the most recorded shark bites in the United States. But this isn't because Florida's waters are uniquely dangerous—it's because Florida hosts extraordinary numbers of surfers, swimmers, and waders across hundreds of miles of coastline year-round.

## Actual Risk Remains Minuscule

Despite rising raw numbers, Burgess and other researchers emphasize that the *rate* of attacks relative to time spent in the water remains extraordinarily low. The odds of a fatal shark encounter are dwarfed by risks from drowning, sunburn-related skin cancer, or even the drive to the beach.

## A Call for Better Reporting

The implication for journalism and public understanding is significant. Framing shark attack statistics without population context can fuel disproportionate fear, potentially harming shark conservation efforts even as it fails to accurately convey real risk. Burgess's work has pushed researchers and reporters alike to consider not just how many attacks occurred, but how many people were exposed to the possibility—and how rarely, even then, an encounter turns dangerous.

As beach tourism continues to grow globally, understanding this population-driven context isn't just an academic exercise—it's essential for accurately communicating risk to a public that often reacts to sharks with fear disproportionate to the actual danger they pose.
